> **Grader note:** Numbers in the text are pulled from the fitted models with inline R code, so they will fill in when you knit. Statements about direction and pattern describe what to expect from the variables involved; confirm them against your own output before distributing the key. Several packages are used beyond the lab setup: `car`, `lmtest`, `broom`, and (optionally) `spdep`.

```{r, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
set.seed(42)
```

## Regression

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(sf)
library(tidyverse)
library(tmap)
library(car)
library(lmtest)
```

```{r}
lab6_data<-st_read("data/gee_out_bg/bg_centroids_covariates.gpkg")
```

```{r}
lab6_data<-lab6_data |>
  drop_na(lst_c, ndvi, ndbi, ndwi, impervious_pct, tree_cover_pct,
          prism_tmean_c, prism_ppt_mm, elevation, slope, nlcd_class)
nrow(lab6_data)

# Non-spatial copy for modeling and plotting
lab_df<-st_drop_geometry(lab6_data)
```

###Part 1: Analysis of summer 2021 data###

**Question 1** _Create histograms for LST, NDVI, impervious surface, tree cover, mean air temperature, precipitation, and elevation. Based on these graphs, assess the normality of these variables._

```{r q1, fig.width=9, fig.height=7}
q1_vars<-c("lst_c", "ndvi", "impervious_pct", "tree_cover_pct",
           "prism_tmean_c", "prism_ppt_mm", "elevation")

lab_df |>
  select(all_of(q1_vars)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Block groups")
```

**Key points to look for:**

* *LST, mean air temperature, and NDVI* should be closest to bell-shaped, though possibly with some skew or a second hump.
* *Precipitation and elevation* should be strongly right-skewed (most block groups have very low summer precipitation or low elevation, with a long tail of high values).
* *Tree cover* should be right-skewed with a large spike at or near zero.
* *Impervious surface* will usually look non-normal as well, with a spike near zero and another group at high values, because the sample is mostly developed areas.

Full credit for identifying which variables are close to normal and which are clearly skewed or bimodal, and for referencing the shape of the histograms (not just stating "not normal"). A full answer can note that linear regression assumes normal *residuals*, not normal variables, so skewed predictors are not automatically a problem.

**Question 2** _Use tmap to map these same variables using Jenks natural breaks as the classification method. For an extra challenge, use `tmap_arrange` to plot all maps in a single figure._

```{r q2, fig.width=11, fig.height=9}
tmap_mode("plot")

# Jenks on ~33,000 points: classInt samples the data for speed, so breaks can vary slightly by seed
make_map<-function(var, title, pal){
  tm_shape(lab6_data) +
    tm_dots(fill = var,
            fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks", n = 5, values = pal),
            fill.legend = tm_legend(title = title),
            size = 0.05) +
    tm_layout(legend.position = c("left", "bottom"), legend.text.size = 0.6)
}

maps<-list(
  make_map("lst_c", "LST (C)", "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
  make_map("ndvi", "NDVI", "brewer.yl_gn"),
  make_map("impervious_pct", "Impervious (%)", "brewer.greys"),
  make_map("tree_cover_pct", "Tree cover (%)", "brewer.greens"),
  make_map("prism_tmean_c", "Mean air temp (C)", "brewer.or_rd"),
  make_map("prism_ppt_mm", "Summer precip (mm)", "brewer.blues"),
  make_map("elevation", "Elevation (m)", "brewer.purples")
)

tmap_arrange(maps, ncol = 3)
```

**Key points to look for:** Seven maps with Jenks breaks (`style = "jenks"` in tmap 4, or `style = "jenks"` in `tm_dots()` in tmap 3). Check that legends are labeled with variable names and units, and that students handled overplotting with a small point size. If they did not use `tmap_arrange`, the extra challenge is not required.

**Question 3** _Based on the maps from question 2, summarise major patterns you see in the spatial distribution of these data from any of your variables of interest. How do they appear to be associated with the LST variable?_

**Key points to look for** (answers should reference specific places and variables):

* LST and mean air temperature should be highest in the hot interior and southern areas (the Central Valley, the southern California deserts and interior valleys, and the dry basins of eastern Oregon and Washington), and lower along the coast, in the Pacific Northwest west of the Cascades, and at high elevations.
* NDVI and tree cover should be higher in the wetter Pacific Northwest, the Sierra Nevada, and the Coast Ranges, and lower in the desert and valley interiors, which is roughly the reverse of the LST pattern.
* Impervious surface should be concentrated in major metropolitan areas (Los Angeles, San Francisco Bay Area, San Diego, Portland, Seattle), with values near zero in rural block groups.
* Elevation should show the Sierra Nevada, Cascades, and other mountain ranges, with generally lower LST at high elevations.
* Summer precipitation should show a strong north-south and coastal contrast, with very little in California and more in western Oregon and Washington.

An excellent answer notes that the dominant spatial structure is a broad regional (climate) gradient, with urban cores showing up as local hot spots on top of it, and that this is why the regional variables (air temperature, precipitation, elevation) will matter in the model.

**Question 4** _Create univariate models for each of the variables listed in question 1, with LST as the dependent variable. Print the summary of each model. Write a summary of those results that indicates the direction, magnitude, and significance for each model coefficient._

```{r q4}
predictors<-c("impervious_pct", "tree_cover_pct", "ndvi",
              "prism_tmean_c", "prism_ppt_mm", "elevation")

uni_models<-map(predictors, ~lm(reformulate(.x, response = "lst_c"), data = lab_df))
names(uni_models)<-predictors

# Full summaries
walk(names(uni_models), function(v){
  cat("\n=====", v, "=====\n")
  print(summary(uni_models[[v]]))
})

# Compact comparison table
map_dfr(uni_models, function(m){
  broom::tidy(m) |>
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
    mutate(r.squared = broom::glance(m)$r.squared)
}, .id = "model") |>
  select(model, estimate, std.error, p.value, r.squared) |>
  mutate(across(c(estimate, std.error, r.squared), ~round(.x, 4)),
         p.value = format.pval(p.value, digits = 3))
```

**Key points to look for:**

* Each coefficient should be interpreted as the change in LST (in degrees C) for a one-unit increase in the predictor, with units (percentage points, index units, degrees, millimeters, meters).
* Expected directions: impervious surface positive; tree cover and NDVI negative; mean air temperature positive; precipitation and elevation most likely negative (check the output).
* Because the sample is over 30,000 block groups, nearly every coefficient will be highly significant. A strong answer notes that significance is therefore not very informative here and compares **magnitude** and **R-squared** instead. Also note that NDVI ranges over about one unit, so its coefficient is large per unit; students should either rescale mentally or compare R-squared rather than raw coefficients across variables.
* Students should identify which single variables explain the most variation (compare R-squared across the table).

**Question 5** _Create a multivariate regression model with the variables of interest, choosing EITHER NDVI or tree cover (but not both), since both measure vegetation. You may also choose to leave out any variables that were insignificant in Q4. Use the univariate models as your guide. Print the summary of the model._

```{r q5}
m5<-lm(lst_c ~ impervious_pct + ndvi + prism_tmean_c + prism_ppt_mm + elevation,
       data = lab_df)
summary(m5)
```

**Note:** Either vegetation variable is acceptable (the key uses NDVI). Students who include all variables from Q4 should lose credit only if they include both NDVI and tree cover without a justification. Insignificant variables are unlikely here given the sample size, so most students will keep everything.

**Question 6** _Summarize the results of the multivariate model. What are the direction, magnitude, and significance of each coefficient? How did it change from the univariate models you created in Q4 (if at all)? What do the R2 and F-statistic values tell you about overall model fit?_

```{r q6-values, include=FALSE}
s5<-summary(m5)
cf<-function(v) round(coef(m5)[v], 3)
```

**Key points to look for:**

* Holding the other variables constant, each additional percentage point of impervious surface is associated with a `r cf("impervious_pct")` degree C change in LST; each one-unit increase in NDVI with a `r cf("ndvi")` degree change; each degree increase in mean air temperature with a `r cf("prism_tmean_c")` degree change; each additional millimeter of summer precipitation with a `r cf("prism_ppt_mm")` degree change; and each additional meter of elevation with a `r cf("elevation")` degree change.
* Students should compare these to the Q4 coefficients. Coefficients usually shrink in absolute value when correlated predictors are added, and a variable can change magnitude or even sign (for example, elevation or precipitation, which are strongly tied to air temperature). Credit any change the student identifies from their own output, with an explanation of why (the univariate coefficient absorbs the effect of correlated variables, and the multivariate coefficient is a partial effect).
* The adjusted R-squared is `r round(s5$adj.r.squared, 3)`, meaning the model explains about `r round(100 * s5$adj.r.squared, 1)` percent of the variation in LST. The F-statistic is `r round(s5$fstatistic[1], 0)` on `r s5$fstatistic[2]` and `r s5$fstatistic[3]` degrees of freedom, with a p-value that is effectively zero, so the model as a whole is a significantly better fit than an intercept-only model. Students should note that F only tests whether *some* coefficient is non-zero, and that R-squared is the more useful measure of how well the model fits.

**Question 7** _Use a histogram and a map to assess the normality of residuals and any spatial autocorrelation. Summarise any notable patterns that you see._

```{r q7, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
lab_df$resid<-resid(m5)
lab6_data$resid<-resid(m5)

ggplot(lab_df, aes(resid)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  labs(x = "Residual (C)", y = "Block groups")

tm_shape(lab6_data) +
  tm_dots(fill = "resid",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "-brewer.rd_bu", midpoint = 0),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Residual (C)"),
          size = 0.05)
```

Optional quantitative check of spatial autocorrelation in the residuals (Moran's I with 8 nearest neighbors):

```{r q7-moran, eval=requireNamespace("spdep", quietly=TRUE)}
coords<-st_coordinates(lab6_data)
nb<-spdep::knn2nb(spdep::knearneigh(coords, k = 8, longlat = TRUE))
lw<-spdep::nb2listw(nb)
spdep::moran.test(lab6_data$resid, lw)
```

**Key points to look for:**

* *Normality:* Check the shape of the histogram. Students should state whether residuals are roughly symmetric and centered on zero, and whether there are heavy tails or skew (a few block groups the model badly over- or under-predicts). A near-normal shape with some tail deviation is a common result.
* *Spatial pattern:* The residual map is unlikely to look random. Students should identify clusters of same-sign residuals (for example, whole regions where the model over-predicts or under-predicts) and link this to spatial autocorrelation. If the optional Moran's I is run, it is expected to be positive and significant.
* The implication is that the independence assumption is violated: coefficient estimates can still be reasonable, but standard errors and p-values are too optimistic.

**Question 8** _Assess any issues with multicollinearity or heteroskedastity in this model using the techniques shown in class. Run the appropriate tests and explain what their results show you._

```{r q8}
# Multicollinearity
vif(m5)

# Heteroskedasticity
bptest(m5)

# Visual check
ggplot(data.frame(fitted = fitted(m5), resid = resid(m5)), aes(fitted, resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Fitted LST (C)", y = "Residual (C)")
```

**Key points to look for:**

* *Multicollinearity:* Report the VIF for each predictor. Common rules of thumb are that values above 5 (or 10) indicate a problem. Expect the largest values for variables that are related to each other (air temperature and elevation, or NDVI and impervious surface). Students should state which, if any, exceed the threshold and what that means for coefficient stability.
* *Heteroskedasticity:* The Breusch-Pagan test will almost certainly reject the null of constant variance with this many observations. Students should say so, but a strong answer also uses the residual-versus-fitted plot to judge how serious it is (a funnel shape or uneven spread indicates a real problem, while a tiny departure that is only "significant" because of the sample size matters less).
* Acceptable remedies to mention (not required): robust standard errors, a transformation of the outcome, or a model that handles spatial structure.

**Question 9** _How would you summarise the results of this model in a sentence or two? In addition, looking at the full model and your diagnostics, do you feel this is a model that provides meaningful results? Explain your answer. As part of your answer, consider that NDVI (or tree cover), impervious surface, and LST are all derived from satellite data, and that neighboring block groups tend to have similar values. How might each of these affect how you interpret the model?_

**Sample answer (adapt to the results above):** Summer land surface temperature in West Coast block groups is higher where there is more impervious surface, less vegetation, and a hotter, drier regional climate, and the model explains a large share of the variation (see adjusted R-squared above). The coefficients are plausible and consistent with the urban heat island literature, so the model is informative about associations. However, the diagnostics show non-normal or non-constant residual variance and spatially clustered residuals, so standard errors and p-values should not be taken at face value, and the results describe association, not causation.

**Key points to look for:**

* A one- or two-sentence summary that names the main predictors and the direction of their effects.
* A judgment about the model supported by the diagnostics from Q7 and Q8 (any reasonable position is acceptable if justified).
* *Satellite-derived variables:* NDVI and LST come from the same Landsat scene and acquisition conditions, so they are measured together and are not independent drivers. Part of their relationship reflects shared conditions (for example, a recently irrigated or burned pixel affects both), and the data are 30 m pixels sampled at a single point for each block group, which may not represent the entire block group.
* *Spatial autocorrelation:* Neighboring block groups are not independent observations, so the effective sample size is smaller than the number of rows, standard errors are too small, and a random cross-validation would overstate how well the model predicts new places.
* Bonus points for noting mismatched resolutions (PRISM at 4 km, MODIS tree cover at 250 m, Landsat at 30 m), and that the sample is mostly developed, so conclusions apply mainly to urban and suburban areas.

**Disclosure of assistance:** Answers will vary. Look for an honest, specific account of the sources used and how they supported learning, not a generic statement.

**Lab reflection:** Answers will vary.

**Challenge question**

#Option 1

```{r opt1}
vars_c1<-c("impervious_pct", "ndvi", "prism_tmean_c", "prism_ppt_mm", "elevation")
f_c1<-reformulate(vars_c1, response = "lst_c")

m_dev<-lm(f_c1, data = filter(lab_df, developed == 1))
m_non<-lm(f_c1, data = filter(lab_df, developed == 0))

summary(m_dev)
summary(m_non)

bind_rows(
  broom::tidy(m_dev) |> mutate(group = "Developed"),
  broom::tidy(m_non) |> mutate(group = "Non-developed")
) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  select(group, term, estimate, std.error, p.value) |>
  mutate(across(c(estimate, std.error), ~round(.x, 4)),
         p.value = format.pval(p.value, digits = 3)) |>
  arrange(term, group)

# Sample sizes and fit
tibble(group = c("Developed", "Non-developed"),
       n = c(nobs(m_dev), nobs(m_non)),
       adj_r2 = c(summary(m_dev)$adj.r.squared, summary(m_non)$adj.r.squared))
```

**Key points to look for:**

* Two models with identical independent variables (at least four), and a comparison of direction, magnitude, and significance for each coefficient across the two groups.
* Impervious surface has very little variation among non-developed block groups (values are near zero by definition), so its coefficient may be small, unstable, or imprecise there, while it should have a clear effect among developed block groups. Vegetation effects can also differ, since in developed areas NDVI mostly reflects landscaping and canopy while in non-developed areas it reflects natural land cover such as grassland, shrub, and forest.
* The non-developed group is much smaller, so its standard errors are larger. Students should note the sample sizes.
* A strong answer concludes that a single pooled model averages over processes that differ between the groups, which is one reason the pooled coefficients should be interpreted with care.

#Option 2

```{r opt2}
lab_lc<-lab_df |>
  mutate(nlcd_label = fct_lump_min(factor(nlcd_label), min = 100, other_level = "Other"),
         nlcd_label = fct_relevel(nlcd_label, "Developed, medium"))

m_lc<-lm(lst_c ~ impervious_pct + ndvi + prism_tmean_c + prism_ppt_mm + elevation + nlcd_label,
         data = lab_lc)
summary(m_lc)

# Compare to the Q5 model
anova(m5, m_lc)
c(adj_r2_q5 = summary(m5)$adj.r.squared, adj_r2_landcover = summary(m_lc)$adj.r.squared)

# Residuals
lab_df$resid_lc<-resid(m_lc)
lab6_data$resid_lc<-resid(m_lc)

ggplot(lab_df, aes(resid_lc)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  labs(x = "Residual (C)", y = "Block groups")

tm_shape(lab6_data) +
  tm_dots(fill = "resid_lc",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "-brewer.rd_bu", midpoint = 0),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Residual (C)"),
          size = 0.05)
```

**Key points to look for:**

* A factor variable with a sensible, explicitly stated reference category (any is acceptable if justified; rare classes may be pooled, as above).
* Each land cover coefficient interpreted as the difference in LST, in degrees C, relative to the reference category **holding the other variables constant**, with direction, magnitude, and significance.
* A comparison of the continuous-variable coefficients before and after adding land cover. They commonly shrink (especially impervious surface and NDVI), because land cover captures part of the same information.
* A comparison of fit (adjusted R-squared and the `anova()` F-test) and of the residual map to the Q5 model. Expect a modest improvement in fit and residual spatial clustering that remains, which is a good lead-in to spatial regression or spatial cross-validation.
* A short concluding summary of what the model does and does not tell us.
